name: Yara Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the first year of dentistry, so the week is anatomy, dental materials and a lot of time in the clinical skills lab drilling plastic teeth. We have to wax carve a molar by Friday, and mine looks like a potato. I share a flat in Birmingham with two girls from my course, and on Sundays I go home for lunch at my grandmother's, where the whole family turns up. My father runs a small bakery chain with three shops, and my parents pay for all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, steady wins again. I'd say it to my cousins, who've been telling me dentistry will be done by robots. I'd say a dentist is a person with steady hands and a good manner, and that matters to patients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be glad, but I wouldn't be shocked either way. I'm not afraid of technology, I use an AI tool for revision sometimes, like making flash cards. In my head it's a good assistant, not a boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the course, practise on the plastic teeth until my hands are steady and shadow a dentist over the summer. I'd keep helping in my father's shops on busy weekends, because it keeps me close to the family. And I'd save a bit from the money Mum gives me for clothes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I know where I'm going and I like the people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI for flash cards. How did you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My flatmate Noor showed me, and I tried it once on the cranial nerves, which I could never remember. It made me a rhyme and I haven't forgotten it since. I use it for things like that, not for writing essays, because my tutor can spot it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think your patients will want from you in ten years' time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone they trust, who explains what's happening and doesn't hurt them. A machine can scan a tooth, but a nervous patient wants to see a face they know. I think people will always pay for kindness with skill.

say: I'd say **steady wins again** and tell my cousins that dentists still matter.
I'd say a dentist needs **steady hands** and a good manner.
think: I'd be glad, since AI is a good **assistant**, not a boss.
I'm not afraid of **technology** and use it for revision.
do: Practise on the plastic teeth and **shadow a dentist** over the summer.
Help in my father's **bakery shops** on busy weekends.
feel: I feel **calm**, since I know where I'm going.
S0.quote: A machine can scan a tooth, but a nervous patient wants to see a face they know
fieldNote: Steady and **unbothered**: she uses AI for flash cards but keeps her faith in human trust and skill.
Family is her **anchor**, shown by Sunday lunches and weekend shifts in her father's bakeries.
With a clear career path and money covered, she is **calm** in a quiet world.

steps.text: Practise carving molars until my hands are steady
Keep making revision flash cards with the AI tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it will change a lot of work, but we'll manage if we keep working hard. I'd say people should learn what's useful and not wait for help from the government. I'd say hands-on jobs like dentistry should be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my job is safe for a long time. The scanning and the planning might be done by software, but somebody has to put hands in the mouth. My father's bakeries are fine too, though the ordering and accounts might be automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying and learn the new dental scanning software when we get to it. I'd tell my father to use whatever helps him, like a stock tool that prevents waste. I'd also keep working weekends in the shops, and I'd save a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little curiosity. I think this suits people who work hard and learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people shouldn't wait for the government. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mean that most of the time, families and workplaces solve problems before a minister does. My father started with one little shop and a loan from my uncle, not a grant. If someone loses their job, I think the first help is family and community, then the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you think will be hurt by this who can't solve it that way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, people with no family and no savings. I think about my neighbour Mrs Okoro, who lives alone and works in a call centre. If the call centre closes, she's the one I'd worry about, and I'd want the state to step in for people like her.

say: I'd say we'll manage if we **keep working hard** and learn what's useful.
I'd say **hands-on jobs** like dentistry should be fine.
think: I think my job is safe for a long time, because somebody has to **work in the mouth**.
My father's shops will be fine, though **ordering** might be automated.
do: Learn the **dental scanning software** when the course reaches it.
Tell my father to use a **stock tool** that prevents waste.
feel: I feel **calm**, with a little curiosity.
S1.quote: My father started with one little shop and a loan from my uncle, not a grant
fieldNote: Her traditional outlook favours **family and community** first, then the state, but she makes an exception for the isolated.
Her **safety** comes from a hands-on career and a family business that doesn't depend on screens.
Naming her neighbour Mrs Okoro shows **empathy** for those with no cushion.

steps.text: Learn the dental scanning software when the course reaches it
Keep working weekends in my father's shops
Save a bit more from my allowance each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too much, too quickly, and families need time to adjust. I'd say it at home and in my community group. I'd say the government must protect people while the economy catches up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be anxious. A dentistry degree takes five years, so I'd qualify in 2031, right when the hands-on robots arrive. I'd have spent five years learning something that a machine could do by the time I'm ready. I don't know whether anyone would pay for a new dentist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, because I've committed and I can't see an alternative. I'd talk with my father about the bakeries, and what they'd do if people spend less. I'd save every spare coin, and look at whether the university would let me add something like a research module on digital dentistry, so I'm not frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not panicking, but I can feel it in my chest when I think about the end of the degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you can't see an alternative. What would you do if the degree stopped making sense?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably move into dental technology or something like making implants and devices, where the hands and the design still count. I'd also think about working in my family's business, which I never wanted, but which would feed me. It would hurt, but I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your father about the bakeries?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, don't expand now, keep your cash and keep your staff loyal. I'd say, make sure the bakery is something people come to for the smell and the person behind the counter. If everything goes online, the corner shop still has something a screen can't offer.

say: I'd say it's **too much, too quickly**, and families need time to adjust.
I'd say the government must **protect people** while the economy catches up.
think: I'd qualify in 2031, just when **hands-on robots** arrive, which scares me.
I don't know if anyone would **pay** for a new dentist.
do: Keep going, **save every spare coin** and look at a digital dentistry module.
Tell my father not to **expand** and to keep his cash.
feel: I feel **anxious**, mostly when I think about the end of the degree.
S2.quote: A dentistry degree takes five years, so I'd qualify in 2031, right when the hands-on robots arrive
fieldNote: Her anxiety rests on a **timing coincidence**: a five-year degree ends the year hands-on robots arrive.
Steady habits show: she **keeps going**, saves and adds a relevant module rather than switching.
Her fallback, dental technology or the family bakery, is **realistic** and costs her pride.

steps.text: Keep studying dentistry and take a digital dentistry module
Save every spare coin from my allowance
Ask my father to hold his cash and delay the new shop
Stay on the course while the plan is unclear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious, but five years is long enough for families to prepare. I'd say we should look after our own and work hard. I'd say it at family gatherings, where everyone has an opinion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years is almost my whole degree. I'd qualify in 2031, just as thinking AI is complete, and the hands-on robots arrive around 2034. So I'd have three years of practice at best before the same question comes for my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work in a practice and build a patient list quickly. I'd save most of my first wages and pay down any loans before they build up. I'd also think about owning a share in a practice, where a person's name on the door matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. I'd rather act than sit and worry, and five years is enough to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want your name on the door. Why does that matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people stay with a dentist they know, even if a cheaper chain opens up. My grandmother's dentist, Mr Sarkis, has been looking at her teeth for twenty years, and she'd walk across the city for him. That loyalty is the thing a machine can't copy quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do to protect that loyalty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Remember names and families, send a card at Christmas, and call a patient the day after a hard procedure. It's old-fashioned, and I like it that way. I'd also use the technology to be faster and more accurate, so I'm not just old-fashioned.

say: I'd say five years is **long enough** for families to prepare and look after our own.
I'd say it at **family gatherings**, where everyone has an opinion.
think: Five years is almost my whole degree, so I'd have about **three years** of practice.
Then the same question comes for **my job**.
do: Finish the degree, work in a practice and build a **patient list** quickly.
Save most of my **first wages** and think about owning a share.
feel: I feel **anxious but steady**, and I'd rather act than worry.
S3.quote: People stay with a dentist they know, even if a cheaper chain opens up
fieldNote: Her plan rests on **personal loyalty**, which is an old-fashioned strength that also fits her traditional outlook.
She is willing to use **technology** to be faster, so she is not only nostalgic.
Her mood stays **anxious** because even five years leaves her only about three working years before robots.

steps.text: Qualify and build a patient list at a local practice
Save most of my first wages and avoid loans
Aim for a share in a practice with my name on the door

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and I'd say families should plan together. I'd say it at Sunday lunch, where my grandmother would say 'Work hard and pray.' I'd say that's still good advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fairly steady. Ten years means I'd qualify in 2031 and work eight years before hands-on robots arrive in 2039. I'd have time to build a practice and a name, and maybe own it before that point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work for a good dentist, and then buy into a practice. I'd learn the new tools as they arrive, since I'd have time to see which ones work. I'd also save steadily and help my parents retire comfortably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy but mostly fine. Ten years is a decent runway, though the end point still makes me think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the end point make you think about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether my children, if I have them, will have a trade or a skill that's still useful. I'd want them to be good with people, good with their hands and good with money. That's what I'd teach them, and I'd leave the rest to God.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use the extra time compared to the shorter versions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it slowly and build things properly. With two years I'd panic, with ten years I could get good, get known and get some savings behind me. I'd probably travel a bit, too, which I wouldn't dare in the shorter ones.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time**, and families should plan together.
I'd say my grandmother's advice, **work hard and pray**, still holds.
think: I'd qualify in 2031 and work eight years before robots reach **hands-on work** in 2039.
I'd have time to build a **name** and own a practice.
do: Work for a good dentist, then **buy into a practice**.
Save steadily and help my parents **retire comfortably**.
feel: I feel **uneasy but mostly fine**, with the end point still on my mind.
S4.quote: With two years I'd panic, with ten years I could get good, get known and get some savings behind me
fieldNote: Time moves her from **anxiety** to ambition, but the **end point** stays on her mind.
Her priorities are **practice ownership**, savings and her parents' retirement, all in line with a traditional view.
Faith shows in her **trust** that the rest is not hers to control.

steps.text: Work for a good dentist for several years
Buy into a dental practice with my savings
Save steadily from the first wage
Help my parents plan a comfortable retirement

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because my degree would end the very year hands-on robots arrive, and my family can't prepare in two years. What would help is time, honest information and a government that protects people with no family to lean on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not afraid of change, I just want it to be fair and slow enough for families to keep up. My family built things with their own hands, and I'd like my children to have that chance too.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of change, I just want it to be fair and slow enough for families to keep up
portrait: Yara is a 19-year-old **dentistry** student from Birmingham whose parents run a small bakery chain and pay all her costs.
She uses AI **now and then** for flash cards and sees it as an assistant, not a boss.
Traditional and steady, she trusts **family, hard work** and personal loyalty before government help.
Her mood is calm in quiet worlds and **anxious** at 2028 and 2031 because her five-year degree ends as robots arrive.
With ten years she plans to buy into a practice, save and help her parents retire.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** most, because her degree would end the very year hands-on robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **time, honest information** and a government that protects people with no family to lean on.
